newsitem.title: UK: Angerstein cuts marine exposure in soft mkt.
newsitem.headline: Angerstein cuts marine exposure in soft mkt.

text.p: Angerstein Underwriting Trust Plc has reduced the amount of marine business it underwrites in the current highly competitive global insurance market.

"We're going softly, softly in this market. We've reduced our exposure in marine...We've expanded in non-marine specialist areas, but there's not been a huge swing," James Illingworth, director of operations, told Reuters after the company announced half-year results.
Angerstein is one of the original 12 corporate capital investors allowed into the Lloyds of London insurance market in 1994.
Rates for most classes of insurance have fallen steadily since reaching a cyclical high in 1994, with marine seeing the most aggressive price cuts.
"The market is exceedingly competitive, probably as competitive as the late 1980s," Illingworth said, adding that Angerstein had not been complacent while premium rates had been falling.
A more selective underwriting stance this year, with the number of Lloyd's insurance syndicates supported by Angerstein reduced to 67 from 70, reflected this strategy, Illingworth said.
Angerstein's overall premium limit -- the maximum amount of premium it can underwrite -- is only slightly higher this year at 197.5 million stg than last year's 192.5 million.
The late 1980s led to some of the worst losses in Lloyd's history, but Illingworth said that changes in the market structure since then made a repetition of those problems unlikely.
Market consolidation had created fewer, larger and better managed players with closer control over their market exposures than during the 1980s, he said.

Failure to keep track of their exposures to certain large risks, such as the Piper Alpha oil platform, landed some syndicates with crippling losses in the late 1980s in a phenomenon known as the spiral.
Illingworth said there was no sign of the return of insurance spirals, adding that Lloyd's syndicates were currently able to obtain very good reinsurance deals.
Most of this reinsurance was purchased outside Lloyd's -- another change from the 1980s when much reinsurance stayed in the market and sometimes concentrated rather than spread liabilities.
Finally, the Lloyd's market was no longer weighed down with pre-1992 liabilities following the launch last year of the Equitas reinsurance company for all old business.
Illingworth said another key plank of its underwriting strategy was to select good underwriters.
"You choose your underwriter rather than your market sector. The best underwriters will always make money in any market."
